## Response

<!-- RESPONSE-START -->
I recently saw a headline that said something like, “Teens who use social media are more likely to be depressed.” At first, it sounds like social media causes depression, but after learning about the research in the Chapter course pack, I realized that claim isn’t automatically true. The chapter explains that to prove causation, researchers need three things: the cause has to happen before the effect (temporal ordering), the two things have to be related (association), and there can’t be another explanation for the results (non-spuriousness). In the social media example, there might be an association—maybe teens who use social media more also report feeling more depressed. That checks one of the boxes. But we still don’t know which came first. Did social media cause the depression, or were teens already feeling depressed and used social media more because of it? There could also be a third factor causing both. For example, teens dealing with loneliness, anxiety, or tough family situations might turn to social media and also experience that depression. In that case, social media isn’t the cause—it’s just connected to something deeper going on. The chapter gives similar warnings with topics like violent video games and aggression, showing that surveys alone can’t prove one thing causes another. To actually claim that social media causes depression, researchers would need a true experiment with random assignment, manipulation of the independent variable, and tight control over the environment. Overall, the headline might show a correlation, but without an experimental design that proves the correct order of events and rules out other explanations, it’s not accurate to say social media directly causes teen depression.
<!-- RESPONSE-END -->

## Word Count & Range Check

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
get_response_text <- function() {
  f <- knitr::current_input()
  if (is.null(f) || !file.exists(f)) return("")
  x <- readLines(f, warn = FALSE)
  # Find the lines that EXACTLY match the start/end markers
  s <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-START -->$", x)
  e <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-END -->$", x)
  if (length(s) != 1 || length(e) != 1 || e <= s) return("")
  paste(x[(s + 1L):(e - 1L)], collapse = "\n")
}
count_words <- function(txt) {
  # Remove code blocks and inline code before counting
  txt <- gsub("```[\\s\\S]*?```", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  txt <- gsub("`[^`]*`", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Keep letters, numbers, spaces, hyphens, and apostrophes
  txt <- gsub("[^\\p{L}\\p{N}\\s'-]", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Split by whitespace and count non-empty words
  words <- unlist(strsplit(txt, "\\s+", perl = TRUE))
  words <- words[nzchar(words)]
  length(words)
}
txt <- get_response_text()
n <- count_words(txt)
minw <- as.integer(params$word_min)
maxw <- as.integer(params$word_max)
in_range <- n >= minw && n <= maxw
cat(sprintf("**Word count:** %d  \n", n))
cat(sprintf("**Required range (%s):** %d–%d words  \n",
            toupper(params$course), minw, maxw))
cat(if (in_range) "**Status:** ✅ In range\n" else "**Status:** ❌ Out of range\n")
```
